case.label: C
case.text: A Network Load Balancer with a lambda target group looks like a lighter, faster entry point for small JSON requests, but the existing entry point is the Application Load Balancer and the rest of the application must stay unchanged, so a second load balancer would need new DNS and routing. A target group of type lambda belongs to the Application Load Balancer, so the case is weak.

answers.flag: Option A also stops direct internet access (the security group allows HTTP only from the VPC CIDR, which covers the load balancer), so only the phrase 'MOST secure' separates D from A; a candidate could also argue that D alone already meets the requirement and B is extra.

case.label: A
case.text: Limiting HTTP to the VPC CIDR removes the 0.0.0.0/0 rule, so no internet client can reach port 80 of the instances, and the load balancer nodes, which sit inside the VPC, can still reach them. Combined with option B (private subnets, no public IPs) the instances have no direct internet path at all, and the work is small. It is less tight than a rule that references the load balancer security group, but the stem only says 'stop all direct access', and A achieves that.

case.label: C
case.text: An EventBridge-driven Lambda function that terminates unhealthy targets does automate replacement, because the Auto Scaling group launches a new instance after termination. It works with no change to the group settings, but it is custom code to build and maintain, so it loses on the least-overhead constraint.

case.label: D
case.text: One Network Load Balancer with TLS listeners is also a single load balancer and would cost less than six. But it needs six different ports, so users could no longer reach each application at the current URL on port 443, and it has no host-header rules. The case fails on the constraint 'current URL'.

case.label: E
case.text: A second Network Load Balancer in Availability Zone B with Route 53 failover records, together with instances in zone B (option A), also survives the loss of zone A. It needs health checks, DNS records and TTL waiting, so it has more parts than adding a subnet to the existing load balancer; the stem's 'LEAST operational overhead' is what rules it out.

case.label: B
case.text: Three load balancers, each with one certificate, satisfy encryption on port 443 and keep every website separate. But the stem already has one load balancer with host-based rules, so this triples the load balancers and DNS work; it only loses on the least-overhead constraint.

answers.flag: The stem does not say that a /health page already exists; if it must be created, B needs an application change and a release just like D. Also A (TCP) would turn the targets healthy with no code change, although it shows less of the real state.

case.label: D
case.text: Making / return HTTP 200 fixes the cause directly: the default health check expects 200 on the path /, and the health check would then match the page that real users load. It needs no change to the load balancer. A candidate can say it is the same effort as creating a /health page, and avoids a second page to keep correct. Its cost is that it removes the sign-in redirect that the application now uses, which the stem does not allow or forbid.

case.label: C
case.text: A Gateway Load Balancer and a fleet in each VPC does pass all traffic through appliances and scales, and it keeps each VPC independent. The stem asks for central management and a central security VPC, so one fleet per VPC multiplies the appliances to manage.

case.label: B
case.text: Business partners calling from their own networks may need fixed addresses to allow-list, and a Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP address in front of an Application Load Balancer gives fixed addresses and path routing. The stem states no need for fixed addresses and asks for MOST cost-effective, and this option adds a second load balancer, so it is weaker.

case.label: A
case.text: Reverse proxy instances with Elastic IP addresses give fixed addresses and keep the path rules on the Application Load Balancer. They work but they are instances to patch, scale and replace, so they lose on least overhead to a Network Load Balancer with the load balancer as its target.

case.label: C
case.text: One internet-facing load balancer with a /app/* rule uses a single load balancer and scales each tier through its own target group. It would make the application tier reachable from the internet through that path, which the stem forbids, so only a very loose reading of 'unreachable' could defend it.

case.label: B
case.text: Adding 4 instances in Availability Zone A makes 6 instances in each zone, so each default Network Load Balancer node splits connections evenly. It costs 4 extra instances, ends with 12 instances instead of the 8 in the stem, and must be repeated whenever the fleet changes, so it loses on the overhead constraint.

case.label: C
case.text: An Auto Scaling lifecycle hook that is completed only after the uploads finish gives the instance exactly as much time as it needs, with no guessed number. It is the standard way to hold an instance until its own work is done. It needs a script and permissions, so it has more overhead than changing one target group attribute.

case.label: C
case.text: ACM managed renewal sounds like the automatic fix with no new work. It applies to ACM-issued public certificates; an imported certificate is not renewed by ACM, which is the cause of the outage in the stem, so this option repeats the problem.

case.label: C
case.text: A Network Load Balancer with Elastic IP addresses that targets an Application Load Balancer gives fixed addresses and also keeps path routing for a later /api/* split. The stem does not ask for path routing, and the MOST cost-effective constraint makes the second load balancer an unneeded cost.

case.label: C
case.text: A Network Load Balancer with a TLS listener and a TLS target group encrypts both hops with ACM and instance certificates, and a candidate may read 'URL path' loosely. But a Network Load Balancer works at the connection level and cannot route by URL path, so it fails the routing requirement.

case.label: C
case.text: Moving session data to ElastiCache is the better long-term design because sessions survive the loss of an instance. The stem asks for a fix as soon as possible with minimal code changes, and this option changes the application code, so it fails the constraint.

case.label: B
case.text: Associating a new security group with the existing load balancer is the smallest change, if the reader assumes that every load balancer can get security groups later. For a Network Load Balancer created without security groups, the documentation says they cannot be associated later, so this option cannot be done and a new load balancer is needed.

case.label: A
case.text: A fixed response on port 80 does tell users to use HTTPS and needs no application change. Users still have to retype the address, so they do not 'reach the HTTPS site' automatically; the permanent redirect in C does that.

case.label: D
case.text: Waiting for health checks needs no action. The stem says the slow instances still pass their health checks, so the load balancer would not stop routing and the incident would continue.

answers.flag: Options C and D also protect every hop and the instances decrypt the (re-encrypted) traffic with their own certificates; only the words 'decrypt the client traffic' (end-to-end TLS pass-through) separate B from D and C, so a candidate who reads 'client traffic' loosely can defend D.

case.label: D
case.text: An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an HTTPS target group encrypts the client hop with an ACM certificate and the second hop again, and every instance uses its own certificate and private key to decrypt what it receives. This meets 'protect the data in transit on every network hop' and 'each instance decrypts with its own certificate', and it adds Layer 7 features such as inspection and routing that pass-through lacks, so it can be called more secure than blind pass-through.

case.label: C
case.text: A separate session database on an EC2 instance also makes the web tier stateless, so sessions survive the loss of a web instance. It is a single instance that the company must run, patch and back up, and it is a new single point of failure, so it is less scalable and has more operational overhead than a managed cache.
